draft.title: A personal activity plan
card: A personal activity plan is a written plan to help one person be more active and sit less. It is built around that person's own goals, such as feeling fitter or joining a team.
choosing clear targets and a time frame, such as walking for 20 minutes on four days each week for six weeks.
recording what you actually do, such as steps or sessions, in a diary or on an app. The record shows whether you are on track.

Both are self-management skills. The person uses the record to check progress against the goals and then changes the plan if needed. Plans also aim to cut long periods of sitting, not only to add exercise.
draft.remember: A good plan starts with the person's goals and uses a record of what they do to check progress.

a.q: Which action is an example of self-monitoring in a personal activity plan?
opts: Logging each day's steps in an app
Setting a target of 8000 steps a day
Joining a local council walking group
Reading about the benefits of walking
a.why: Self-monitoring means recording what you actually do, so the step log shows progress. Setting a target of 8000 steps is goal setting, which is tempting but is about choosing a target, not recording results.
a.clue: Which one records what has already happened?

b.q: Priya wants to run 5 km at a fun run. Each week she writes down her runs and compares them with her plan. After three weeks she has missed half her sessions, so she moves them to times that suit her. What does this show?
opts: Using self-monitoring to check progress and adjust the plan
Setting a goal, which is the only skill the plan needs
Following a plan that must stay the same once it is written
Replacing her own goal with the goal of a population program
b.why: Priya records what she does, compares it with her plan and changes the plan, which is self-monitoring used to adjust. Setting the goal was the first step, but the plan also needs a record to check progress. The card says plans can be changed if needed.
b.clue: What did she do with the weekly record?

a.best: Logging each day's steps in an app

b.best: Using self-monitoring to check progress and adjust the plan

problems.detail: Two distractors use absolute words ('must stay the same', 'the only skill') where the card says the plan is changed 'if needed'. A student can rule them out on wording alone, which narrows the choice without knowing the idea.

b.q: Priya wants to run 5 km at a fun run in eight weeks. Each week she writes down her runs and compares them with her plan. After three weeks she has missed half her sessions. She keeps the same target but moves her runs to times that suit her better. What does this show?
opts: Using self-monitoring to check progress and adjust the plan
Using goal setting to pick a harder target and time frame
Comparing her running with other runners in her area
Cutting long periods of sitting during her working week
b.why: Priya records her own runs, checks them against her plan and then changes when she runs, which is self-monitoring used to adjust the plan. Goal setting is tempting, but she kept the same 5 km target and eight-week time frame, so she did not set a new goal.
b.clue: Did her target change, or only when she runs?
